claim: In most vertebrate neurons, action potentials are triggered at the distal end of the axon initial segment (AIS).
source: In most vertebrate neurons, action potentials are triggered at the distal end of the axon initial segment (AIS).
evidence: This is stated as an established fact in the abstract without specific citation, drawing from general scientific knowledge.

claim: Both position and length of the AIS vary across and within neuron types, with activity, development and pathology.
source: Both position and length of the AIS vary across and within neuron types, with activity, development and pathology.
evidence: This is stated as an established fact in the abstract, drawing from general scientific knowledge.

claim: A distal shift of the AIS normally produces a modest increase in excitability.
source: A distal shift of the AIS normally produces a (modest) increase in excitability
evidence: This is a primary finding of the theoretical analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: The pattern of increased excitability with distal AIS shift can reverse if a hyperpolarizing current is present at the AIS, due to resistive coupling with the soma.
source: but we explain how this pattern can reverse if a hyperpolarizing current is present at the AIS, due to resistive coupling with the soma.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the theoretical analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: The theory of neural excitability was developed on the space-clamped giant squid axon.
source: Historically, the theory of neural excitability was developed on the space-clamped giant squid axon (Hodgkin and Huxley, 1952a)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Hodgkin and Huxley, 1952a.

claim: The giant squid axon stems from a syncytium (many cells merging their axons into a giant one).
source: which stems from a syncytium (many cells merging their axons into a giant one) (Young, 1936).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Young, 1936.

claim: Spikes generally initiate in the axon initial segment (AIS) in vertebrate neurons.
source: Spike initiation occurs in a different configuration in vertebrate neurons: spikes generally initiate in the axon initial segment (AIS), a small structure next to the soma (Bender and Trussell, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Bender and Trussell, 2012.

claim: The fact that spikes initiate in the AIS has been known for a long time.
source: Although this fact has been known for a long time (Coombs et al., 1957)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Coombs et al., 1957.

claim: The fact that spikes initiate in the AIS has been generally neglected in theory.
source: it has been generally neglected in theory (Koch, 1999; Tuckwell, 1988a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Koch, 1999 and Tuckwell, 1988a.

claim: Both the position and length of the AIS can vary not only across cells but also with activity.
source: Recently, its potential functional significance has been emphasized by a number of studies showing that both the position and length of the AIS can vary not only across cells (Hamada et al., 2016; Höfflin et al., 2017; Kuba et al., 2006), but also with activity (Grubb et al., 2011; Jamann et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to empirical studies.

claim: AIS movements could be involved in the regulation of excitability.
source: These observations raise the possibility that AIS movements could be involved in the regulation of excitability.
evidence: This is presented as a speculative possibility based on the observations cited.

claim: Variations of AIS geometry co-occur with changes in excitability and many other factors.
source: Variations of AIS geometry indeed co-occur with changes in excitability, but also with many other factors (Kole and Brette, 2018), such as changes in input resistance (Grubb and Burrone, 2010; Hatch et al., 2017; Lezmy et al., 2017; Wefelmeyer et al., 2015), phosphorylation of voltage-gated sodium (Nav) channels (Evans et al., 2015), redistribution of voltage-gated potassium (Kv) channels (Kuba et al., 2015), or changes in cell capacitance (Kuba et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to empirical studies.

claim: In some studies, distal displacement of the AIS is associated with decreased excitability.
source: In some studies, distal displacement of the AIS is associated with decreased excitability (Grubb and Burrone, 2010; Hatch et al., 2017; Lezmy et al., 2017; Wefelmeyer et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to empirical studies.

claim: In some studies, neurons with more distal AIS have an identical or slightly hyperpolarized threshold.
source: In others, neurons with more distal AIS have an identical (Thome et al., 2014) or slightly hyperpolarized threshold (Hamada et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to empirical studies.

claim: It is challenging to experimentally isolate the specific contribution of AIS geometry to excitability changes.
source: Thus, it is challenging to experimentally isolate the specific contribution of AIS geometry to excitability changes.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the mixed results described in previous sentences.

claim: Theoretical work proposed that increased electrical isolation of the AIS from the large soma should result in increased excitability.
source: Theoretical work proposed that increased electrical isolation of the AIS from the large soma should result in increased excitability (Baranauskas et al., 2013; Brette, 2013; Telenczuk et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to theoretical studies.

claim: Several numerical studies have reported decreased excitability when the AIS is moved distally, depending on cell morphology or on the expression of Kv channels in the AIS.
source: However, several numerical studies have reported decreased excitability when the AIS is moved distally, depending on cell morphology (Gulledge and Bravo, 2016) or on the expression of Kv channels in the AIS (Lezmy et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to numerical modeling studies.

claim: The relation between AIS position and excitability is highly nonlinear, since even the direction of change depends on model parameters.
source: These findings indicate that the relation between AIS position and excitability is highly nonlinear, since even the direction of change depends on model parameters.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the contradictory findings in modeling studies.

claim: Differences in excitability have been reported using various measures: rheobase, current density threshold or voltage threshold at the soma.
source: Finally, differences in excitability have been reported using various measures: rheobase, current density threshold or voltage threshold at the soma.
evidence: This is stated as an observation about the literature.

claim: It has been argued that a more relevant quantity is the axonal threshold, since spikes initiate in the AIS.
source: It has also been argued that a more relevant quantity is the axonal threshold, since spikes initiate in the AIS (Yu et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Yu et al., 2008.

claim: When the axon is small compared to the somatodendritic compartment, an axonal current produces a larger local depolarization when it is applied further from the soma.
source: When the axon is small compared to the somatodendritic compartment, an axonal current produces a larger local depolarization when it is applied further from the soma, while the converse holds when the axon is large.
evidence: This is a theoretical finding derived from cable theory analysis in the manuscript.

claim: When the axon is large compared to the somatodendritic compartment, an axonal current produces a smaller local depolarization when it is applied further from the soma.
source: When the axon is small compared to the somatodendritic compartment, an axonal current produces a larger local depolarization when it is applied further from the soma, while the converse holds when the axon is large.
evidence: This is a theoretical finding derived from cable theory analysis in the manuscript.

claim: The physiological situation is that the axon is small compared to the somatodendritic compartment.
source: We show with neuroanatomical and electrophysiological data that the physiological situation is the former one.
evidence: This is supported by neuroanatomical and electrophysiological data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Excitability changes caused by changes in the AIS are captured by the somatic voltage threshold.
source: In the second part, we show that excitability changes caused by changes in the AIS are captured by the somatic voltage threshold (and not, perhaps counter-intuitively, by the AIS threshold).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the theoretical analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: Excitability changes caused by changes in the AIS are not captured by the AIS threshold.
source: In the second part, we show that excitability changes caused by changes in the AIS are captured by the somatic voltage threshold (and not, perhaps counter-intuitively, by the AIS threshold).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the theoretical analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: The somatic voltage threshold can be expressed as a function of AIS geometry, Nav conductance density and non-sodium current at the AIS.
source: From this analysis, we derive a parsimonious mathematical expression for threshold variations as a function of AIS geometry, Nav conductance density and non-sodium current at the AIS.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the theoretical analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: When the AIS is moved away from the soma, the cell becomes slightly more excitable, unless a strong hyperpolarizing current is present at the AIS.
source: We find that, when the AIS is moved away from the soma, the cell becomes slightly more excitable, unless a strong hyperpolarizing current is present at the AIS.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the theoretical analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: In the sealed end condition with a very small soma, the input resistance is approximately R(x) ≈ raλ - x.
source: More precisely, we can calculate that R(x)≈raλ-x, where ra is axial resistance per unit length (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is derived from cable theory and shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Moving the AIS away from the soma should make the cell slightly less excitable in the sealed end condition.
source: Thus, moving the AIS away from the soma should make the cell slightly less excitable.
evidence: This is an inference from the cable theory analysis for the sealed end condition.

claim: When the somatodendritic compartment is small, the neuron is most excitable when the AIS is next to the soma.
source: This is consistent with the findings of Gulledge and Bravo (2016), who observed numerically that when the somatodendritic compartment is small, the neuron is most excitable when the AIS is next to the soma.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Gulledge and Bravo (2016).

claim: In the killed end condition with a large soma, the input resistance increases with the distance of the injection site.
source: It follows that the input resistance increases with the distance of the injection site, which would tend to make the cell more excitable when the AIS is moved away from the soma, since less Na+ current is then required to produce the same depolarization.
evidence: This is derived from cable theory analysis for the killed end condition.

claim: In the killed end condition, the soma is a current sink.
source: We express this fact by stating that the soma is a current sink.
evidence: This is a theoretical characterization of the killed end condition.

claim: The current flowing toward the soma produces a linear depolarization between the soma and the injection site, with a total voltage difference ΔV = rax·I.
source: The current I flowing toward the soma produces a linear depolarization between the soma and the injection site, with a total voltage difference ΔV=rax.I.
evidence: This is derived from cable theory analysis for the killed end condition.

claim: On a short time scale, the somatic depolarization is negligible because the soma charges much more slowly than the axon.
source: However, this difference holds for the stationary response. On a short time scale, the somatic depolarization is negligible because the soma charges much more slowly than the axon.
evidence: This is illustrated in Figure 2A and supported by the analysis.

claim: The voltage gradient between the soma and the injection site essentially follows Ohm's law: ΔV = RaI.
source: The difference between the two responses, which is the voltage gradient between the soma and the injection site, essentially follows Ohm's law: ΔV=RaI (Figure 2B), where Ra=rax is the axial resistance of the axon between soma and injection site
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2B and derived from the analysis.

claim: The axon charges faster than the soma for a broad range of distances of the axonal stimulation site.
source: This plot shows quantitatively that the axon indeed charges faster than the soma, for a broad range of distances of the axonal stimulation site.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2C and supported by the analysis.

claim: The case with a large soma is characterized by two key properties: 1) a current injected at the axon produces a resistive voltage gradient between the soma and injection site, proportional to the axial resistance Ra; 2) the axonal site charges much faster than the soma.
source: To summarize, the case with a large soma is characterized by two key properties: 1) a current injected at the axon produces a resistive voltage gradient between the soma and injection site, proportional to the axial resistance Ra of that piece of axon; 2) the axonal site charges much faster than the soma.
evidence: This is a summary of the theoretical analysis for the large soma case.

claim: The regime with a large soma is called the resistive coupling regime.
source: We call this regime the resistive coupling regime (Brette, 2013; Kole and Brette, 2018; Telenczuk et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a definition with supporting citations.

claim: Layer 5 cortical pyramidal neurons have a soma of about 30 µm diameter attached to a large apical dendrite and an AIS of about 1–1.5 µm diameter.
source: These neurons have a soma of about 30 µm diameter attached to a large apical dendrite and an AIS of about 1–1.5 µm diameter (Hamada et al., 2016; Höfflin et al., 2017)
evidence: This is supported by citations to empirical studies.

claim: A voltage gradient develops very quickly between the soma and injection site in layer 5 cortical pyramidal neurons when a current pulse is injected in the axon.
source: Figure 2D shows the response to a current pulse injected at 75 µm away from the soma, in the soma and at the axonal injection site. As in the theoretical case described above, a voltage gradient develops very quickly between the soma and injection site (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2D and 2E from experimental recordings.

claim: The axonal input resistance increases with distance of the injection site in layer 5 cortical pyramidal neurons.
source: As noted by Hu and Bean (2018), the axonal input resistance increases with distance of the injection site.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Hu and Bean (2018) and shown in the data.

claim: The passive properties of layer 5 cortical pyramidal neurons follow the resistive coupling regime.
source: Therefore, the passive properties of these neurons follow the resistive coupling regime, rather than the small soma regime (compare with Figure 1B).
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental data analysis.

claim: Cerebellar granule cells have a small cell body of about 6 µm diameter and very thin axons of diameter about 0.2 µm.
source: However, those simulations were performed with a constant AIS diameter of 1.5 µm. As noted in Telenczuk et al. (2017), cerebellar granule cells, which have a small cell body of about 6 µm diameter (Delvendahl et al., 2015) also have very thin axons, of diameter about 0.2 µm (Perge et al., 2012; Wyatt et al., 2005)
evidence: This is supported by citations to empirical studies.

claim: Cerebellar granule cells still follow resistive coupling theory because the soma remains large compared to the axon.
source: and as a result they still follow resistive coupling theory because the soma remains large compared to the axon.
evidence: This is an inference based on the dimensional analysis and cited data.

claim: Smaller neurons tend to have a smaller AIS.
source: The data show that smaller neurons also tend to have a smaller AIS.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3 with neuroanatomical data.

claim: The correlation between AIS and soma diameter appears both within and across cell types.
source: The correlation between AIS and soma diameter appears both within and across cell types
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3 with neuroanatomical data.

claim: Small neurons have a thin AIS such that electrical properties are preserved.
source: In summary, small neurons also have a thin AIS, such that electrical properties are preserved.
evidence: This is an inference from the dimensional analysis and neuroanatomical data.

claim: The passive properties of the soma-AIS system should generically follow the resistive coupling regime.
source: This indicates that the passive properties of the soma-AIS system should generically follow the resistive coupling regime.
evidence: This is an inference from the dimensional analysis and neuroanatomical data.

claim: In the resistive coupling regime, the appropriate measure of excitability for studying the effect of AIS structural plasticity is the somatic voltage threshold.
source: We will now show that in this regime, the appropriate measure of excitability for studying the effect of AIS structural plasticity is the somatic voltage threshold.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the theoretical analysis.

claim: The biophysical model reproduces a high amplitude action potential that initiates first in the AIS where it rises quickly (dV/dt > 1,000 V/s), then appears in the soma with a distinct kink and a biphasic phase plot.
source: First, a high amplitude action potential initiates first in the AIS where it rises quickly (dV/dt > 1,000 V/s), then appears in the soma with a distinct kink and a biphasic phase plot (Figure 4C,D; Kole et al., 2008; Kole and Stuart, 2008; Naundorf et al., 2006; Stuart et al., 1997; Yu et al., 2008).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4C,D and supported by citations to empirical studies.

claim: Na+ and K+ currents have little overlap at spike initiation in the biophysical model.
source: Second, Na+ and K+ currents have little overlap at spike initiation (Figure 4E,F; Hallermann et al., 2012), which implies that Kv channels are more involved in repolarization than in spike initiation.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4E,F and supported by a citation to Hallermann et al., 2012.

claim: Kv channels are more involved in repolarization than in spike initiation.
source: which implies that Kv channels are more involved in repolarization than in spike initiation.
evidence: This is an inference from the observation of little overlap between Na+ and K+ currents at spike initiation.

claim: Both rheobase and current density threshold vary not only with changes in the AIS but also with the neuron's input resistance.
source: However, an issue with both rheobase and current density threshold is that they vary not only with changes in the AIS but also with the neuron's input resistance.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 5A and B.

claim: Grubb and Burrone (2010) reported an increase of about 50% in threshold current density after long-term depolarization associated with a distal displacement of the AIS.
source: For example, Grubb and Burrone (2010) reported an increase of about 50% in threshold current density after long-term depolarization associated with a distal displacement of the AIS.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Grubb and Burrone (2010).

claim: Grubb and Burrone (2010) had to discount the estimated effect of an observed reduction of input resistance (about 1/3) to infer the specific effect of changes in the AIS.
source: To infer the specific effect of changes in the AIS, they had to discount the estimated effect of an observed reduction of input resistance (about 1/3).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Grubb and Burrone (2010).

claim: Changes in rheobase reflect excitability changes due to factors in the AIS and elsewhere.
source: Thus, changes in rheobase reflect excitability changes due to factors in the AIS and elsewhere.
evidence: This is an inference from the analysis shown in Figure 5A and B.

claim: In the resistive coupling regime, the somatic voltage threshold is a measure of excitability that depends only on axonal factors.
source: In the resistive coupling regime, the somatic voltage threshold is a measure of excitability that depends only on axonal factors.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the theoretical analysis.

claim: The somatic voltage threshold is defined as the maximum somatic membrane potential that can be reached without triggering a spike.
source: It is defined as the maximum somatic membrane potential that can be reached without triggering a spike (Brette, 2013).
evidence: This is a definition with a supporting citation.

claim: The voltage threshold varies with G in the same way as the rheobase.
source: This is illustrated in Figure 5A and B: the voltage threshold varies with G in the same way as the rheobase (more precisely, Vthreshold-V0 is proportional to the rheobase), but it does not vary with gL.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5A and B.

claim: The voltage threshold does not vary with somatic leak conductance gL.
source: This is illustrated in Figure 5A and B: the voltage threshold varies with G in the same way as the rheobase (more precisely, Vthreshold-V0 is proportional to the rheobase), but it does not vary with gL.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5A and B.

claim: When the Na+ current enters the AIS, it depolarizes the AIS very rapidly, while at the time scale of spike initiation the soma does not get charged significantly.
source: The reason is the separation of time scales between somatic and axonal dynamics, due to the size difference: when the Na+ current enters the AIS, it depolarizes the AIS very rapidly, while at the time scale of spike initiation the soma does not get charged significantly.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2C and F and explained by the analysis.

claim: At the relevant time scale, the somatic potential acts as a fixed boundary condition for the axon.
source: It follows that at the relevant time scale, the somatic potential acts as a fixed boundary condition for the axon.
evidence: This is an inference from the separation of time scales.

claim: The initiation of a spike depends only on the somatic potential and properties of the axon, but not on properties of the soma or dendrites.
source: Therefore, the initiation of a spike depends only on the somatic potential and properties of the axon, but not on properties of the soma or dendrites (an exception is the axon-carrying dendrite of some neurons, Kole and Brette, 2018).
evidence: This is an inference from the analysis, with a noted exception.

claim: In terms of dynamical systems theory, the somatic potential is a bifurcation parameter.
source: In terms of dynamical systems theory, the somatic potential is a bifurcation parameter (see below).
evidence: This is a theoretical characterization.

claim: A hyperpolarizing current at the distal end of the AIS raises the somatic threshold in proportion to the hyperpolarizing current.
source: As a result, the somatic voltage threshold is raised in proportion of the hyperpolarizing current.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5C.

claim: A hyperpolarizing current at the distal end of the AIS represents a reduction of excitability, because the rheobase also increases.
source: This change does represent a reduction of excitability, because the rheobase also increases
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The voltage threshold at the AIS changes in the opposite direction when a hyperpolarizing current is injected at the AIS, and does not capture the change in excitability.
source: In contrast, the voltage threshold at the AIS changes in the opposite direction (Figure 5C): it does not capture the change in excitability due to this particular change at the AIS, but on the contrary it is misleading.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The somatic voltage threshold specifically captures the axonal factors of excitability.
source: We note for now that the somatic voltage threshold specifically captures the axonal factors of excitability.
evidence: This is an inference from the analysis.

claim: The Na+ current changes approximately exponentially with voltage below threshold.
source: The Na+ current changes approximately exponentially with voltage below threshold (Baranauskas and Martina, 2006; Hodgkin and Huxley, 1952b): INa∝Gexp⁡V/k⁡, where G is the total available Na+ conductance and k is the Boltzmann slope factor of Nav channels (typically 4–8 mV Angelino and Brenner, 2007; Platkiewicz and Brette, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to empirical studies.

claim: For an axon with constant section, the axial resistance Ra is proportional to AIS position Δ.
source: For an axon with constant section (e.g. cylindrical), the axial resistance Ra is proportional to AIS position Δ.
evidence: This is a standard result from cable theory.

claim: The theoretical formula for point AIS threshold is essentially correct in a simplified cable model that includes leak currents, axonal capacitive currents and Nav activation dynamics.
source: Figure 6C and D show that the formula is essentially correct in this case.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6C and D.

claim: In the biophysical model, the spike threshold is more sensitive to Nav conductance than predicted (logarithmic slope of about 9 mV instead of k = 5 mV).
source: The numerical results show quantitative differences with the theoretical predictions (Figure 6E and F), namely, the spike threshold is more sensitive to Nav conductance than predicted (logarithmic slope of about 9 mV instead of k = 5 mV).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6E and F.

claim: Theory correctly predicts that shifting the AIS distally or increasing total Nav conductance lowers spike threshold on a logarithmic scale.
source: Nonetheless, theory correctly predicts that 1) shifting the AIS distally or increasing total Nav conductance lowers spike threshold on a logarithmic scale, 2) the two logarithmic factors interact linearly (meaning the plotted lines are parallel).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6E and F.

claim: The relation between threshold and AIS position is quantitatively well predicted (logarithmic slope of about 6–7 mV).
source: The relation between threshold and AIS position is also quantitatively well predicted (logarithmic slope of about 6–7 mV).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6E.

claim: The threshold is lowered when the AIS is moved away from the soma.
source: As expected, the threshold is lowered when the AIS is moved away from the soma (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7A.

claim: The relation between threshold and AIS position is less steep for an extended AIS than for a point AIS.
source: However, the relation is less steep than in the case of a point AIS.
evidence: This is shown by comparing Figure 7A with Figure 6E.

claim: The threshold is lowered when the AIS is extended.
source: The threshold is also lowered when the AIS is extended (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The spike threshold of an extended AIS starting at the soma is the same as for a point AIS placed at position Δ = L with the same total number of Nav channels, except for a constant term difference of 0.87 k.
source: Remarkably, this is the same formula as for a point AIS placed at position Δ = L and with the same total number of Nav channels. The only difference is the constant term. By solving the differential equation analytically, we find that this difference is 0.87 k (about 4.3 mV with k = 5 mV)
evidence: This is derived from the theoretical analysis.

claim: The spike threshold of the extended AIS is almost the same as for a point AIS with the same number of channels placed in the middle of the AIS.
source: An equivalent and more intuitive way to understand this result is to note that a threshold shift of 0.87 k is equivalent to a displacement of the AIS by a factor e-0.87 ≈ 0.42. In other words, the spike threshold of the extended AIS is almost the same as for a point AIS with the same number of channels placed in the middle of the AIS (Figure 8A, green curve)
evidence: This is derived from the theoretical analysis and shown in Figure 8A.

claim: Extending the AIS lowers the spike threshold by two mechanisms: by increasing the number of Nav channels and by moving the initiation site away from the soma.
source: This analysis shows that extending the AIS lowers the spike threshold by two mechanisms: by increasing the number of Nav channels and by moving the initiation site away from the soma.
evidence: This is an inference from the theoretical analysis.

claim: Compressing or extending the AIS around its middle position x1/2 without changing the total Nav conductance has very little effect on the theoretical spike threshold.
source: Figure 8B shows that compressing or extending the AIS around its middle position x1/2 without changing the total Nav conductance has very little effect on the theoretical spike threshold.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 8B.

claim: In the simulated biophysical model, the effect of compressing or extending the AIS around its middle position is more significant but remains small.
source: In the simulated biophysical model, the effect is more significant but remains small (Figure 8C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 8C.

claim: With an extended AIS, the spike threshold is approximately the same as that of the equivalent point AIS placed at the middle position x1/2, with the same total Nav conductance.
source: Therefore, we find that with an extended AIS, the spike threshold is approximately the same as that of the equivalent point AIS placed at the middle position x1/2, with the same total Nav conductance.
evidence: This is a summary of the theoretical finding.

claim: The variation of spike threshold can be separated into three independent contributions: g, L, and x1/2.
source: The remarkable finding is that the variation of spike threshold can be separated into three independent contributions.
evidence: This is a primary theoretical finding.

claim: The theoretical finding that spike threshold variation can be separated into three independent contributions is essentially valid in the biophysical model.
source: Figure 9 indicates that this theoretical finding is essentially valid in the biophysical model.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 9.

claim: The observed slopes in the biophysical model are close to the theoretical prediction k = 5 mV for the geometric factors x1/2 and L (6–7 mV), and a little larger for g (8–9 mV).
source: The observed slopes are close to the theoretical prediction k = 5 mV for the geometric factors x1/2 and L (6–7 mV), and a little larger for g (8–9 mV).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 9.

claim: The theoretical effect of AIS start position on excitability is significant but moderate.
source: Thus, the theoretical effect of AIS start position on excitability is significant but moderate.
evidence: This is an inference from the theoretical analysis.

claim: For realistic changes in position and length, the theory predicts moderate changes in threshold.
source: Thus, for realistic changes in position and length, the theory predicts moderate changes in threshold, consistently with empirical observations in structural plasticity studies (see Discussion).
evidence: This is an inference from the theoretical analysis.

claim: When a strong Kv7 conductance is placed along the AIS, moving the AIS away from the soma makes the neuron less excitable in the biophysical model.
source: Specifically, Lezmy et al. (2017) observed in a biophysical model that when a strong Kv7 conductance is placed along the AIS, moving the AIS away from the soma makes the neuron less excitable. This effect can be observed in our model if we add a strong hyperpolarizing conductance on the distal half of the AIS (Figure 10A).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Lezmy et al. (2017) and shown in Figure 10A.

claim: The voltage threshold measured at distal end of the AIS still follows the theoretical prediction when a hyperpolarizing conductance is present, with spikes initiating at lower axonal voltage when the AIS is moved away from the soma.
source: However, it appears that the voltage threshold measured at distal end of the AIS still follows the theoretical prediction, with spikes initiating at lower axonal voltage when the AIS is moved away from the soma (Figure 10B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 10B.

claim: A hyperpolarizing current I injected at a point AIS will hyperpolarize the AIS relative to the soma by an amount ΔV = RaI = raΔI.
source: By resistive coupling, the current will hyperpolarize the AIS relative to the soma by an amount ΔV=RaI=raΔI (ra is the axial resistance per unit length) (Figure 11A).
evidence: This is derived from the theoretical analysis and shown in Figure 11A.

claim: The voltage threshold at the AIS is not substantially affected by a hyperpolarizing current.
source: As shown on Figure 11B, the voltage threshold at the AIS is not substantially affected by this current (see Materials and methods) – although a hyperpolarizing current may indirectly lower the threshold by deinactivating Nav channels (there is indeed a slight decrease with increasing current amplitude).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 11B.

claim: The somatic threshold increases linearly with a hyperpolarizing current, by an amount equal to ΔV.
source: It follows that the somatic threshold increases linearly with the current, by an amount equal to ΔV.
evidence: This is an inference from the theoretical analysis.

claim: In the absence of hyperpolarizing current, the somatic threshold is theoretically below the AIS threshold by an amount k (about 5 mV).
source: In the absence of hyperpolarizing current, the somatic threshold is theoretically below the AIS threshold by an amount k (about 5 mV).
evidence: This is derived from the theoretical analysis.

claim: The difference between somatic and AIS threshold is predicted to be -k - ΔV when a hyperpolarizing current is present.
source: The difference between somatic and AIS threshold is therefore predicted to be -k-ΔV. This prediction holds in the biophysical model, as shown in Figure 11C
evidence: This is derived from the theoretical analysis and shown in Figure 11C.

claim: When the AIS is moved away from the soma, the spike threshold at the AIS decreases as predicted, but the somatic threshold differs from it by -k - ΔV, which can make it increase with distance.
source: Thus, when the AIS is moved away from the soma, the spike threshold at the AIS decreases as predicted in the previous section, but the somatic threshold differs from it by -k-ΔV, which can make it increase with distance (Figure 11D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 11D and derived from the theoretical analysis.

claim: Hu and Bean (2018) found that in layer 5 pyramidal cells, the AIS is about 3 mV hyperpolarized relative to the soma.
source: Empirically, Hu and Bean (2018) found that in layer 5 pyramidal cells, the AIS (more precisely, the axonal bleb) is about 3 mV hyperpolarized relative to the soma.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Hu and Bean (2018).

claim: The contribution of hyperpolarizing currents to threshold variations should be small in neurons.
source: This suggests that the contribution of this effect to threshold variations should be small.
evidence: This is an inference from the empirical finding by Hu and Bean (2018).

claim: The spike threshold still varies with AIS position as expected when the axon diameter is scaled up.
source: We can see that the spike threshold still varies with AIS position as expected (logarithmic regression slope: 6.8 mV in the original neuron vs. 7.1 mV in the large neuron).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 12A.

claim: If the 500 µm axon is extended to a 1000 µm axon, the spike threshold does not change.
source: If the 500 µm axon is extended to a 1000 µm axon, then the distal axonal resistance Rdistal is barely affected and therefore the spike threshold does not change (Figure 12B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 12B.

claim: If the axon is myelinated, the spike threshold is slightly lowered.
source: However, if the axon is myelinated, so that the specific membrane resistance is increased by a factor 4 (and capacitance decreased by the same factor), then the spike threshold is slightly lowered (Figure 12B, dashed).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 12B.

claim: If the axon is myelinated, the threshold shift due to finite distal axonal resistance should be halved, which implies that the spike threshold should be lowered.
source: Therefore, if the axon is myelinated, then this threshold shift should be halved, which implies that the spike threshold should be lowered.
evidence: This is an inference from the theoretical analysis.

claim: The effect of myelination on spike threshold should be limited.
source: In summary, the effect of myelination on spike threshold should be limited.
evidence: This is an inference from the theoretical analysis and simulations.

claim: An axonal tree is electrically equivalent to an unbranched axon if diameters follow the rule dparent^(3/2) = ddaughter1^(3/2) + ddaughter2^(3/2).
source: In particular, Rall has shown that an axonal tree is electrically equivalent to an unbranched axon if diameters follow the rule dparent3/2=ddaughter 13/2+ddaughter 23/2.
evidence: This is supported by reference to Rall's theory.

claim: When diameters follow Rall's rule, the spike threshold is unchanged.
source: Figure 12C (dashed) shows that indeed in this case the spike threshold is unchanged.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 12C.

claim: Chklovskii and Stepanyants (2003) report an average exponent of about 5/2 for axon branching, with large variability.
source: Empirically, this relation is not always satisfied: Chklovskii and Stepanyants (2003) report an average exponent of about 5/2, with large variability.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Chklovskii and Stepanyants (2003).

claim: When the branching exponent is 5/2, the spike threshold is slightly lowered.
source: In this case, the spike threshold is slightly lowered (Figure 12C, light blue).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 12C.

claim: The spike threshold is almost unchanged for an axo-dendritic neuron compared to the original unbranched axon, for a given axial resistance.
source: Figure 12D shows the spike threshold as a function of axial resistance between the soma and AIS, for a neuron with a dendrite of 2 µm diameter that splits into two equal branches (according to Rall's law), one of which carrying the AIS. The spike threshold is almost unchanged compared to the original unbranched axon, for a given axial resistance.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 12D.

claim: Axon morphology appears to have a small impact on excitability.
source: Overall, axon morphology appears to have a small impact on excitability.
evidence: This is an inference from the analysis of various morphological scenarios.

claim: In neurons of chick nucleus magnocellularis, the AIS elongates by about 10 µm after 7 days of auditory deprivation, with no significant change in AIS start position.
source: In neurons of chick nucleus magnocellularis, the AIS elongates by about 10 µm after 7 days of auditory deprivation, with no significant change in AIS start position (Kuba et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Kuba et al., 2010.

claim: In chick nucleus magnocellularis, it was reported that immunofluorescence intensity did not change after auditory deprivation, which suggests that at least the structural density of Nav channels did not change.
source: It was reported that immunofluorescence intensity did not change, which suggests that at least the structural density of Nav channels did not change.
evidence: This is an inference from the reported immunofluorescence data.

claim: All else being equal, the expected spike threshold shift in chick nucleus magnocellularis after auditory deprivation is -5.2 mV.
source: All else being equal, and in the absence of strong AIS hyperpolarization (e.g. Kv7), we then expect that the spike threshold shifts by −5.2 mV (using k = 5 mV; see Table 2).
evidence: This is calculated from the theoretical formula.

claim: The reported change in spike threshold in chick nucleus magnocellularis after auditory deprivation was −4 mV.
source: The reported change was −4 mV (reported with p<0.05), a fairly good match.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Kuba et al., 2010.

claim: In chick nucleus laminaris, the voltage threshold was found to decrease by −12 to −14 mV between E15 and P3-7.
source: The voltage threshold was found to decrease by −12 to −14 mV between E15 and P3-7, a very large change.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Kuba et al., 2014.

claim: In high frequency neurons of chick nucleus laminaris, AIS geometry changed significantly during development, with a distal shift (13 to 45 µm, start position) and a shortening (26 to 10 µm).
source: AIS geometry also changed significantly in high frequency neurons, with a distal shift (13 to 45 µm, start position) and a shortening (26 to 10 µm).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Kuba et al., 2014.

claim: The theoretical expectation for threshold shift in high frequency neurons of chick nucleus laminaris during development is 0.4 mV.
source: When we combine them, we find a theoretical expectation of 0.4 mV for the threshold shift.
evidence: This is calculated from the theoretical formula.

claim: Observed changes in threshold in chick nucleus laminaris during development are likely due not to changes in AIS geometry but possibly to changes in patterns of expression of ionic channels.
source: We conclude from this analysis that observed changes in threshold are likely due not to changes in AIS geometry but possibly to changes in patterns of expression of ionic channels.
evidence: This is an inference from the discrepancy between theoretical expectations and observed changes.

claim: Nav1.6 channels appear later than Nav1.2 channels during the course of development in some preparations.
source: For example, it has been observed in other preparations that Nav1.6 channels appear later than Nav1.2 channels during the course of development (Boiko et al., 2003)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Boiko et al., 2003.

claim: Nav1.2 channels activate at lower voltage than Nav1.6 channels.
source: and the latter activate at lower voltage (Rush et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Rush et al., 2005.

claim: Chronic depolarization (48 hr) of cultured hippocampal neurons induces a distal shift of the AIS of about 5 µm.
source: Chronic depolarization (48 hr) of cultured hippocampal neurons induces a distal shift of the AIS of about 5 µm (Grubb and Burrone, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Grubb and Burrone, 2010.

claim: Together with a slight shortening of the AIS, theory predicts a modest threshold shift of −1.1 mV for cultured hippocampal neurons after chronic depolarization.
source: Together with a slight shortening of the AIS, theory then predicts a modest threshold shift of −1.1 mV, therefore slightly increased excitability.
evidence: This is calculated from the theoretical formula.

claim: Grubb and Burrone observed a decrease in excitability as measured by threshold current density in cultured hippocampal neurons after chronic depolarization, but it was mostly due to a change in input resistance.
source: The authors observed on the contrary a decrease in excitability as measured by threshold current density, but it was mostly due to a change in input resistance.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Grubb and Burrone, 2010.

claim: The voltage threshold in cultured hippocampal neurons was reported to raise by about 4.3 mV after chronic depolarization, but this was not statistically significant.
source: Nonetheless, the voltage threshold was also reported to raise by about 4.3 mV; this was not statistically significant because of substantial inter-cellular variations in threshold.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Grubb and Burrone, 2010.

claim: In cultured hippocampal dentate granule cells, 3 hr of depolarization produce a shortening of the AIS, for which the expected threshold change is about 2.4 mV.
source: In cultured hippocampal dentate granule cells (Evans et al., 2015), 3 hr of depolarization produce a shortening of the AIS, for which we would expect a threshold raised by about 2.4 mV.
evidence: This is calculated from the theoretical formula and supported by a citation to Evans et al., 2015.

claim: The measured threshold in cultured hippocampal dentate granule cells is lowered by −1.1 mV in normal condition after depolarization, and by −1.9 mV in pro-PKA condition.
source: Instead, the measured threshold is lowered by −1.1 mV in normal condition, and by −1.9 mV in pro-PKA condition (aimed at re-phosphorylating Nav channels). Both changes were not statistically significant.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Evans et al., 2015.

claim: When AIS length and threshold are compared within groups in cultured hippocampal dentate granule cells, a significant negative correlation is found in each case, consistent with theory.
source: However, when AIS length and threshold are compared within groups (with and without chronic depolarization, with and without pro-PKA treatment), a significant negative correlation is found in each case, consistent with theory.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Evans et al., 2015.

claim: In cultured dopaminergic interneurons of the olfactory bulb, one day of chronic depolarization produces a proximal shift and a small elongation of the AIS.
source: Finally, in cultured dopaminergic interneurons of the olfactory bulb, one day of chronic depolarization produces a proximal shift and a small elongation of the AIS (Chand et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Chand et al., 2015.

claim: The theoretical expectation for threshold shift in cultured dopaminergic interneurons of the olfactory bulb after chronic depolarization is a small 0.6 mV shift.
source: As these two factors tend to counteract each other, the theoretical expectation in this case is a small 0.6 mV shift of the threshold.
evidence: This is calculated from the theoretical formula.

claim: The measured change in threshold in cultured dopaminergic interneurons of the olfactory bulb was −0.4 mV (for the biphasic neurons).
source: The measured change was −0.4 mV (for the biphasic neurons), which, given the 1.5 mV standard deviation in measurements, appears consistent.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Chand et al., 2015.

claim: All studies examined in cultured neurons and in development report changes in AIS geometry that are expected to produce small threshold changes (−1 to 2 mV).
source: In summary, all studies that we have examined in cultured neurons and in development report changes in AIS geometry that are expected to produce small threshold changes (−1 to 2 mV).
evidence: This is a summary of the analysis of experimental studies.

claim: In cultured neurons, reported changes in threshold are not statistically significant, which could be interpreted as consistent with the expectation of small changes.
source: In cultured neurons, reported changes are not statistically significant, which could be interpreted as consistent with the expectation.
evidence: This is an inference from the analysis of experimental studies.

claim: In development, there is a large decrease in threshold that seems likely due to changes in expression patterns of ionic channels.
source: In development, there is a large decrease in threshold that seems likely due to changes in expression patterns of ionic channels.
evidence: This is an inference from the analysis of experimental studies.

claim: In the one study examined on structural AIS plasticity in adults, the observed threshold change (4–5 mV) was consistent with expectations.
source: In the one study that we could examine on structural AIS plasticity in adults, the observed threshold change (4–5 mV) was consistent with expectations.
evidence: This is an inference from the analysis of experimental studies.
